title: Transactions in NoSQL
goal: By the end you can explain how a transaction that spans partitions is made atomic (prepare, a recorded decision, commit), predict what DynamoDB, MongoDB and a Cassandra lightweight transaction do when two writers collide, and choose a better data model when a transaction isn't worth its price.

warmup.q: Two MongoDB transactions run at the same time. Both read A-1001's balance of 100.00 and both try to debit it. The second debit is sent while the first transaction is still open. What happens to the second transaction?
options: It waits until the first one commits, then debits the new balance
Its debit fails at once with a write conflict, and the whole transaction has to run again
Both debits apply, and the balance ends up wrong
It succeeds, and the first transaction is aborted instead
warmup.why: MongoDB lets the first writer of a document win and fails the second write at once with `WriteConflict`, labelled `TransientTransactionError`. It doesn't queue it, because its snapshot is already stale: it read 100.00, which is no longer true. The fix is to abort and rerun the whole transaction on a new snapshot. Waiting is what a plain write outside any transaction does when it hits a document an open transaction has changed.

sections.h: One partition is atomic for free; two partitions need a vote
sections.body:
Lesson 4 sent one `TransactWriteItems` that debited A-1001, credited A-2002 and claimed an idempotency key, and DynamoDB applied all of it or none of it. You saw what it costs (two writes per item) and what can cancel it (`TransactionConflict`). Now look at how it's built, because the same problem sits under every store in this lesson. A-1001 and A-2002 are in different partitions, so they can live on different machines. No single machine can make the change atomic by itself.

On one machine, atomic is cheap. A write to one DynamoDB item, one MongoDB document or one Cassandra partition is atomic because one node owns it: it logs the change and applies it, and nobody sees half. Build the two-machine version one step at a time.

Version 1 sends the two writes separately. A crash between them leaves 30.00 debited and never credited, the warm-up of lesson 4.

Version 2 asks first. The coordinator, the process running the transaction, asks each partition "can you do this?", and when both say yes it tells both "do it". But between the yes and the do, another transfer can debit A-1001, and the yes is stale. So a partition that says yes must **hold** the item: refuse other transactions on it until it hears the outcome. That first round is called prepare.

Version 3 fixes the crash in the middle. If the coordinator dies after the yeses and before the "do it", the items stay held and nobody knows the outcome. So the coordinator writes its decision somewhere durable before it sends it, and another coordinator can read it and finish the job. Prepare, record the decision, commit: that's two-phase commit (2PC).

**Atomic across machines means every participant first promises, one decision is written where a crash can't erase it, and only then does anything change.** That's the picture for this lesson. Each store below answers the same three questions differently: who decides, what a participant promises, and where the decision lives.

DynamoDB's answer is in its 2023 USENIX paper. Any coordinator in a fleet can take a transaction and stamps it with a timestamp. A storage node accepts a prepare only if the condition holds, the timestamp is newer than the item's last write, and no other transaction is in flight on the item. Otherwise it rejects, and the coordinator cancels everything. Decisions go into a ledger, itself a DynamoDB table, and a recovery manager finishes stalled ones. Lesson 4's facts fall out of this: two writes per item are the two rounds, and `TransactionConflict` is a rejected prepare. Transactions whose items share one partition skip the two rounds, because one node decides alone.

All three hold, so the node accepts and records T1 next to the item. Nothing has changed yet, but the item is now spoken for.

sections.h: MongoDB: each transaction reads a snapshot, and the first writer wins
sections.body:
Lesson 8 kept a payment and its refunds in one document, so one guarded `updateOne` could check and change them together. When the rule spans documents, say a transfer that changes two account documents and inserts a ledger document, MongoDB has multi-document transactions. They run only on a replica set or a sharded cluster, not on a standalone server; lab Compose files for this track run even a single node as a one-member replica set, `rs0`, for that reason.

Inside a transaction you can read, decide in Kotlin and write, like an Oracle transaction. So how does MongoDB keep two transactions apart? Build it up.

Version 1 locks everything a transaction reads, until it commits. That's two-phase locking, from lesson 8 of the database internals track, "Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI". It's correct, and a long report would block every transfer it touched.

Version 2 is what MongoDB does for reads. Each transaction reads from a **snapshot**: the data as committed when the transaction started. The storage engine keeps old versions for this, the multi-version idea from "MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM" in the same track. Reads never block and are never blocked.

Writes still need a rule. If two transactions change the same document, the second write fails at once with `WriteConflict`. First writer wins, and nobody waits. The error carries the label `TransientTransactionError`, which means: abort and run the whole transaction again. Retrying just the failed statement would be wrong, because the transaction's snapshot no longer matches reality. The Try-it shows tx2 failing, then retrying with a new snapshot that sees tx1's debit, at which point its own condition is false.

The Java driver's `session.withTransaction { }` does this loop for you. It reruns the block on `TransientTransactionError`, retries just the commit on `UnknownTransactionCommitResult`, and gives up after 120 seconds. The lab writes the same loop by hand so you know what it does.

Three limits matter in practice. A plain write outside any transaction that hits a document an open transaction has changed waits until that transaction ends. A transaction must finish within `transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`, 60 seconds by default, or a cleanup task aborts it. And snapshot isolation isn't serializable: two transactions that read the same two balances and each write a different one don't conflict, which is the write skew of "Transactions and isolation levels", lesson 12 of the SQL track. Keep the rule in the documents you write, with guarded updates. Jepsen's 2020 test of MongoDB 4.2.6, from lesson 8, adds one more: set `readConcern: "snapshot"` and `writeConcern: "majority"` on every transaction yourself.

steps: From the `labs` folder, start MongoDB 9.0 as a one-member replica set: `docker compose -f env/mongo.yml up -d --wait`.
Read the script below. Predict what tx2's debit prints, what an outside read sees before tx1 commits, and what tx2 sees when it retries. The last part sleeps for 12 seconds on purpose.
Run it: `docker compose -f env/mongo.yml exec mongo mongosh sfz --quiet /sfz/nosql-10-transactions.js`. Then stop MongoDB: `docker compose -f env/mongo.yml down -v`.

try.expect:
```text
tx1 reads A-1001: 10000
tx2 reads A-1001: 10000
tx1 debit 3000: 1
tx2 debit 8000: WriteConflict ["TransientTransactionError"]
outside, before tx1 commits: 10000
outside, after tx1 commits: 7000
tx2 retry reads A-1001: 7000
tx2 retry debit 8000: 0
outside write: MaxTimeMSExpired after 2028 ms

commit after 12 s: NoSuchTransaction
A-1001 at the end: 7000
```

Both transactions read 10000 from their snapshots. tx1 writes first, so tx2's write fails at once with `WriteConflict` and the label `TransientTransactionError`. Outside, nobody sees tx1's debit until it commits. tx2's retry is a new transaction with a new snapshot: it sees 7000, and its guarded debit of 8000 modifies nothing. The plain write outside a transaction waited for tx1 until its 2-second `maxTimeMS` ran out. With the limit set to 5 seconds, the transaction that slept 12 was aborted by the server's cleanup, so its commit finds `NoSuchTransaction` and its debit never happened: A-1001 is still 7000.

sections.h: Cassandra: Paxos agrees on one value for one partition
sections.body:
Lesson 7 claimed an idempotency key with `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS`, and lesson 6 said why plain quorums can't do that. Two coordinators both read "no row" at `QUORUM`, both write, and last write wins keeps one of them without telling the other. A compare-and-set needs the replicas to agree on one order before anyone writes. Cassandra has no leader to decide, so it runs Paxos, Leslie Lamport's consensus protocol, for that one partition. Lesson 12 of the database internals track, "Replication and consensus with Raft", built Raft, a close relative that elects a leader first.

Build it from the race. Version 1 stamps each attempt with a ballot, a number that grows, and asks the replicas to promise to refuse anything with a lower one. Once a majority has promised ballot 2, an attempt still holding ballot 1 is refused when it tries to write. Any two majorities share a replica, so two attempts can't both hold a majority's promise.

That isn't enough. Say attempt 1 got its value accepted by one replica and then its coordinator died. Attempt 2 can't tell whether that value was already chosen. So every promise also reports any value the replica accepted but never saw committed, and Paxos's one rule says the newcomer must **finish that value before proposing its own**. The second stepper shows it.

Cassandra's lightweight transaction (LWT) is four round trips to a majority of replicas, all visible in the Try-it's trace:

1. Prepare and promise: "Promising ballot".
2. Read the current row and check the `IF`: "Reading existing values for CAS precondition".
3. Propose and accept: "Accepting proposal".
4. Commit, which writes the row into the table: "Committing proposal".

A plain write is one round trip. The Paxos state lives in a table of its own, `system.paxos`, which is why the trace says "Adding to paxos memtable". If the condition is false, you get `[applied] = False` and the current row. The Paxos phases use the serial consistency level, `SERIAL` or `LOCAL_SERIAL`, and a read at `SERIAL` goes through Paxos too, so it sees every applied LWT.

The cost list is short. Each LWT waits for four majority round trips; two clients racing on one partition can keep bumping each other's ballots until one gives up after `cas_contention_timeout` (1 second in the 5.0.9 `cassandra.yaml`). Cassandra 4.1 added Paxos v2, which needs two round trips for a write, but 5.0.9 still ships `paxos_variant: v1` as the default; switching takes a full repair and a rolling restart. And it's one partition only: a batch with an `IF` condition can't span partitions.

sections.h: Accord in 6.0, and when a better model beats a transaction
sections.body:
Cassandra 6.0 adds Accord: transactions across partitions and tables, strict serializable, with no leader. Any node can coordinate, and the common case needs one round trip of consensus. It's alpha. The Docker image `cassandra:6.0-alpha2` exists, the downloads page still lists 5.0 as the newest GA line, and the syntax may change before release. In the alpha, Accord is off until `accord.enabled: true` is set in `cassandra.yaml`, and each table opts in with `transactional_mode = 'full'`. A transaction reads with `LET`, decides with `IF ... THEN`, and writes, between `BEGIN TRANSACTION` and `COMMIT TRANSACTION`. The Try-it moves 30.00 between two partitions of two tables in one statement. Treat it as the direction Cassandra is going, not something to build payments on this year.

Now the harder question: when should you not use a transaction at all? Every tool in this lesson charges something. DynamoDB bills two writes per item and cancels on contention. MongoDB aborts on write conflicts and after 60 seconds. A Cassandra LWT costs four round trips per write. And across services, which is where most of your transfers really run, there's no shared transaction at all.

A better data model often removes the need:

- Put what must change together into one item or document. Lesson 8's refunds array made the refund rule a single guarded update.
- Make one conditional write do the job. An idempotency claim is one `attribute_not_exists` put or one `IF NOT EXISTS`, not a transaction.
- Split a cross-account transfer into steps that are each atomic on one partition, and let a durable workflow drive them to the end: debit A-1001 and record the pending transfer in A-1001's own document, then credit A-2002 idempotently, then mark it done. If the credit can never succeed, a compensating step refunds the debit. That's a saga. Money is visibly "in flight" for a moment, and a reconciliation report can find any transfer that got stuck.

For a transfer between two accounts that the business already treats as pending, use the saga, in a Temporal workflow. Use a transaction when the invariant needs one indivisible step, such as an idempotency claim and the payment it guards, and keep that transaction inside one partition or one document when you can.

MongoDB: transactions, and why data modeling comes first

analogy: A cross-partition transaction is a wedding. The officiant (the coordinator) asks each partner "do you?" and each one, by saying yes, promises not to marry anyone else in the meantime (prepare: the item is held). Only when both have said yes does the officiant pronounce them married and write it in the register (the decision in the ledger), and the register, not anyone's memory, settles the question if the officiant faints halfway. If either says no, there is no wedding at all. Paxos is the same ceremony with no fixed officiant: anyone may run it, the one holding the newest ticket number goes first, and a newcomer who finds a half-finished ceremony must complete it rather than start their own. The analogy breaks in two places: real partners don't get refused for being busy with someone else's ceremony, as a DynamoDB item does, and in a database the whole thing has to finish in milliseconds or be retried.
in_your_world: Your Oracle transfers are one local transaction, and an XA transaction across Oracle and a message queue is two-phase commit with a coordinator in the application server, which is why a crashed JTA coordinator can leave in-doubt transactions for a DBA to resolve. Moving to NoSQL changes where that coordinator lives, not whether you need one. For a wallet in DynamoDB, keep the debit, the ledger entry and the idempotency claim in one `TransactWriteItems`, and expect `TransactionConflict` on a busy merchant account; retry with jitter. In MongoDB, use `withTransaction` and set `snapshot` and `majority` on it. For a transfer between two services, there is no shared transaction: model it as a saga in a Temporal workflow, with each step one atomic, idempotent write keyed by the transfer id from the Kafka command.
mistake: The most common mistake is wrapping a read-then-write in a transaction and assuming the transaction makes it safe, then retrying only the statement that failed. In MongoDB the read came from a snapshot, so when the write fails with `WriteConflict` the decision you made from that read is stale; rerunning just the write either fails again or applies a decision based on old data. In DynamoDB the read was never part of the transaction at all. People do it because a transaction feels like a lock around everything inside it. The fix: put the condition in the write itself (a guarded update or a condition expression), and on `TransientTransactionError` or `TransactionConflict` rerun the whole unit of work, reads included, with the same idempotency key.

compare.note: MongoDB runs a conversation: the session opens a snapshot, your Kotlin reads and decides, and the server checks for write conflicts as the writes arrive. The flexibility costs a retry loop around your own code, which `withTransaction` provides. Accord takes the whole transaction as one statement: reads go in `LET`, decisions in `IF`, and the cluster orders it against every other transaction before running it, so there is no conflict for your code to retry. DynamoDB's `TransactWriteItems` from lesson 4 sits between them: one request, but with no reads at all, only conditions. Because MongoDB lets your code decide between the read and the write, keep the condition in the update's filter as well, as the Kotlin does; the other two decide inside the database.

worked.title: A transfer between two accounts without a cross-partition transaction

steps.say: Start from the requirement and what the business already accepts. A transfer may show as pending for a few seconds; it must never move money twice or lose it. The two accounts are two MongoDB documents, possibly on two shards.
steps.code:
transfer txf-k-1: 30.00 from A-1001 to A-2002
must hold:  never debited twice, never credited twice, never debited without a credit in the end
may happen: A-1001 shows the debit a moment before A-2002 shows the credit

steps.say: Step 1 is one atomic write on A-1001's document: debit it and record the pending transfer inside it. The filter checks the balance AND that this transfer id isn't recorded yet, so a retry modifies nothing.
steps.code:
db.accounts.updateOne(
  { _id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: { $gte: 3000 }, "pending.id": { $ne: "txf-k-1" } },
  { $inc: { balanceMinor: -3000 },
    $push: { pending: { id: "txf-k-1", to: "A-2002", amountMinor: 3000 } } })
// modifiedCount 0: insufficient funds, or already done; read the document to tell which

steps.say: Step 2 is one atomic write on A-2002's document: credit it, guarded by the same transfer id, so running it twice credits once.
Step 3 closes the transfer on A-1001: move it from `pending` to done. If step 2 can never succeed (the account was closed), the compensating step refunds A-1001 instead, guarded the same way.

Something has to run steps 1 to 3 to the end, through crashes and deploys. That is a durable workflow: a Temporal workflow whose activities are these three writes, each safe to retry because each is guarded by the transfer id.
steps.code:
workflow transfer(txf-k-1):
  debit(A-1001)           activity, retried until it answers: done / insufficient
  credit(A-2002)          activity, retried; on permanent failure -> refund(A-1001)
  close(A-1001)           activity, retried
# no step ever holds two documents at once; a crash resumes at the next step

steps.say: Count what you traded. No transaction, so no write conflicts across accounts, no 60-second limit and no two-phase cost. In return: three writes instead of one commit, a moment where the money is visibly in flight, and a workflow engine you must run. For payments that is usually the right trade, because pending already exists in the business.
steps.code:
one transaction           saga of single-document writes
atomic across docs     yes                       no: in flight for a moment
conflicts / retries    the whole transaction     each step on its own
needs                  a replica set, 60 s max   a workflow engine (Temporal)
works across services  no                        yes

steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. `PaxosRegisterTest` needs no Docker; `MongoTransfersTest` starts a one-member MongoDB replica set through Testcontainers (a few seconds, more on the first pull). All fourteen fail.
In `PaxosRegister.kt`, write `Acceptor.prepare` and `Acceptor.accept`. Each is three lines: compare the ballot with `promised`, then remember. The first two tests pass.

Write `compareAndSet` from its KDoc: majority check, prepare, finish any unfinished proposal and start again, read, propose, commit, counting round trips. Seven more pass, including the one where a crashed proposer's value must win and the one that races 300 rounds of claims with lost messages.

In `MongoTransfers.kt`, write `transfer`: one session, a loop of `startTransaction(options)`, the ledger insert, the guarded debit, the credit and the commit, with a retry on `TransientTransactionError`. Five more pass. The conflict test holds a rival transaction open on A-1001 for 300 ms and expects your first attempts to fail and a later one to succeed.
hints: `prepare`: `val p = promised; if (p != null && ballot <= p) return Promise.Rejected(p)`, then set `promised` and return `Promise.Ok(inProgress, committed)`. `accept` refuses only when `proposal.ballot < promised` (equal is fine: it's the proposer that prepared).

In `compareAndSet`, keep `var trips = 0` outside a `while (true)` loop and `continue` after finishing someone else's proposal. Unfinished means: an `inProgress` whose ballot is greater than the highest `committed` ballot among the `Ok` replies.
`highestPromise(replicas)` gives the ballot for `Contended`. `read(replicas)` is the read step.
Mongo: every call takes the session first: `accounts.updateOne(session, filter, update)`. A duplicate ledger id is a `MongoWriteException` with `e.error.category == ErrorCategory.DUPLICATE_KEY`.

Catch `MongoException`, call `abortQuietly(session)`, and if `e.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.TRANSIENT_TRANSACTION_ERROR_LABEL)` sleep `backoff(attempt)` and loop. For the commit, loop while the error has `UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION_COMMIT_RESULT_LABEL`.

drill.title: The transaction retry loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. In Kotlin, write the loop that runs a MongoDB transaction body with the core API: start a session, start a transaction with `snapshot` and `majority`, run `body(session)`, commit, and retry the whole thing on `TransientTransactionError` (up to 10 attempts) and only the commit on `UnknownTransactionCommitResult`. Then say in one sentence why retrying just the failed statement is wrong.

recap: One item, document or partition is atomic because one node owns it. Across partitions, every participant must first promise (prepare), one decision must be recorded durably, and only then does anything change (commit): two-phase commit.

DynamoDB's coordinators prepare each item (condition, timestamp, nobody else in flight), record decisions in a ledger, then commit. A rejected prepare is `TransactionConflict`; nothing waits, so your code retries with backoff.

MongoDB transactions need a replica set, read from a snapshot, and let the first writer of a document win: the loser gets `WriteConflict` with `TransientTransactionError` and must rerun the whole transaction. The default time limit is 60 seconds. Set `snapshot` and `majority` yourself.

A Cassandra lightweight transaction runs Paxos on one partition: prepare and promise, read, propose and accept, commit. Four round trips in 5.0's default v1, against one for a plain write. A newcomer must finish any accepted value it finds.

Accord in Cassandra 6.0 (alpha) adds strict serializable transactions across partitions with `BEGIN TRANSACTION`. Before reaching for any transaction, try one document, one conditional write, or a saga of single-partition steps.

quiz.q: A `TransactWriteItems` that debits a busy merchant's account fails with `TransactionCanceledException`, reason `TransactionConflict` on the debit. What happened inside DynamoDB?
options: The debit's condition was false
The transaction waited for a lock on the item and timed out
Another transaction was in flight on that item, so the storage node rejected the prepare and the whole transaction was cancelled
The debit was applied but the other items were not
quiz.why: A storage node accepts a prepare only if no other transaction is in flight on the item (and the condition and timestamp checks pass). One rejection cancels everything; nothing was written. A false condition would say `ConditionalCheckFailed`. DynamoDB doesn't queue transactions behind each other, which is why the right response is a retry with jittered backoff, not a longer timeout.

quiz.q: A MongoDB transaction reads A-1001 (100.00), decides to debit 80.00, and its `updateOne` fails with `WriteConflict`. A teammate retries just that `updateOne` inside the same session. What's wrong with that?
options: The transaction was aborted and its snapshot is stale; the read and the decision must be redone in a new transaction
Nothing: the update has a guard, so it is safe to retry
Write conflicts are permanent; the transfer must be rejected
The update must be retried outside the transaction
quiz.why: `TransientTransactionError` means "rerun the whole transaction". Another transaction changed A-1001 after this one's snapshot, so the 100.00 it read is no longer true, and any decision based on it has to be made again on a new snapshot. Retrying outside the transaction would lose atomicity with the credit and the ledger insert.

quiz.q: A Cassandra keyspace has three replicas. One is down. An `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` arrives. What happens?
options: It fails: Paxos needs every replica to promise
It runs as a plain insert, because Paxos is skipped while a replica is down
It waits until the third replica returns
It runs: every phase needs a majority, two of three, and two are up
quiz.why: Each Paxos phase waits for a majority of replicas, so one of three can be down. With two down, the coordinator can't reach a majority and the LWT fails as unavailable. Cassandra never quietly downgrades an LWT to a plain write. The replica that was down catches up through repair.

quiz.q: During a lightweight transaction's prepare, one replica's promise reports an accepted value from an older ballot that it never saw committed. What must the new proposer do?
options: Ignore it: an uncommitted value doesn't count
Finish that value first (propose and commit it under its own ballot), then start its own operation again
Abort and return an error to the client
Merge its own value with the old one
quiz.why: That value may already have been accepted by a majority, which makes it chosen, and the proposer can't tell. Paxos's rule is to finish it. Ignoring it is the tempting answer and the one that would let two different values win. The lab's test with a crashed proposer checks exactly this.

quiz.q: From lesson 6: why can't QUORUM reads and QUORUM writes alone give you "claim this idempotency key only if nobody has"?
options: QUORUM reads don't see QUORUM writes
QUORUM writes are rejected when the key exists
Two coordinators can both read "absent" before either writes; both writes succeed, and last write wins keeps one without telling the other
Idempotency keys need ALL, not QUORUM
quiz.why: R + W > N makes reads overlap acknowledged writes, but nothing orders a read and a write from two different clients. Both claims read before either wrote, so both saw no row; both writes are then acknowledged, and timestamps settle the outcome silently. A lightweight transaction adds the missing agreement on order, with Paxos.

flashcards.front: What are the two phases of two-phase commit?
flashcards.back: Prepare: every participant checks and holds its part, and answers yes or no. Commit (or cancel): the coordinator records the decision durably, then tells everyone.

flashcards.front: When does a DynamoDB storage node reject a transaction's prepare?
flashcards.back: When a condition fails, the item would break a limit, the transaction's timestamp isn't newer than the item's last write, or another transaction is in flight on the item (`TransactionConflict`).

flashcards.front: What does `TransientTransactionError` tell your MongoDB code?
flashcards.back: Abort and rerun the whole transaction, reads included, on a new snapshot. A write conflict is the usual cause.

flashcards.front: MongoDB's default limit on a transaction's runtime?
flashcards.back: 60 seconds (`transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`). A periodic cleanup aborts older ones; the commit then fails with `NoSuchTransaction`.

flashcards.front: The four round trips of a Cassandra LWT (Paxos v1)?
flashcards.back: Prepare and promise, read (check the IF), propose and accept, commit. Each waits for a majority of replicas.

flashcards.front: Paxos's one rule for a new proposer?
flashcards.back: If a promise reports an accepted value newer than the last commit, finish that value before proposing your own.

flashcards.front: What is Accord, and can you use it in production today?
flashcards.back: Cassandra 6.0's multi-partition, strict serializable transactions (`BEGIN TRANSACTION ... COMMIT TRANSACTION`). 6.0 is alpha: not yet.

terms.plain: Making a change on several machines atomic: all participants prepare and promise, the coordinator records one decision, then all commit or cancel.
The process that runs a transaction across participants and decides its outcome. DynamoDB keeps a fleet of them and a ledger of their decisions.
Each transaction reads the data as committed when it started. Reads never block; two writers of one item conflict. Write skew is still possible.
Two open transactions writing the same document. MongoDB fails the second write at once and labels the error `TransientTransactionError`.
A consensus protocol: replicas promise ballots and accept proposals so that only one value is chosen, even with crashes and races.
The ever-growing number a Paxos proposer uses; replicas refuse anything lower than what they promised. Cassandra uses a time-based UUID.
Cassandra's compare-and-set on one partition, `IF NOT EXISTS` or `IF col = ...`, run with Paxos. The reply's `[applied]` says whether it happened.
A long operation made of local atomic steps, each with a compensating step, driven to the end by a durable workflow instead of one transaction.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks: "NoSQL has transactions now, so can we just wrap the transfer in one and stop worrying?" Explain what a transaction across partitions has to do, what each of DynamoDB, MongoDB and Cassandra does when two writers collide, and when you'd model the transfer differently.
explain_back.answer: Across partitions no single machine can make the change atomic, so every store does a version of the same thing: each participant first promises (DynamoDB holds the item after a successful prepare, Paxos replicas promise a ballot), one decision is recorded where a crash can't lose it (DynamoDB's ledger, a majority of Paxos replicas), and only then does data change. Collisions are where they differ. DynamoDB rejects the second transaction's prepare and cancels it with TransactionConflict; our code retries with backoff. MongoDB gives each transaction a snapshot and fails the second writer of a document with WriteConflict, labelled TransientTransactionError, so we rerun the whole transaction, reads included; it also aborts anything older than 60 seconds. Cassandra only offers compare-and-set on one partition, a lightweight transaction that costs four Paxos round trips, and Accord for multi-partition transactions is still alpha in 6.0. So transactions exist, but they cost writes, retries and latency, and none spans services. For a transfer between two accounts I'd rather do two single-document conditional writes keyed by the transfer id, a debit that records the pending transfer and an idempotent credit, driven by a Temporal workflow with a compensating refund. I'd keep a transaction for things that must be one step, like an idempotency claim and the payment it guards, ideally inside one partition.

deeper.body:
DynamoDB's paper describes more tricks than this lesson used. Single reads aren't blocked by a prepared transaction: a `GetItem` returns the last committed value and is ordered before the pending transaction. A plain `PutItem` with no condition can even be ordered before a prepared transaction, because the transaction's later write will overwrite it anyway. `TransactGetItems` is "writeless": it reads every item with its log sequence number, reads them again, and succeeds only if nothing changed in between, so a read transaction never writes anything. And items that were deleted are tracked with one maximum-delete timestamp per partition rather than a tombstone per item, which occasionally cancels a transaction that could have run.

Classic two-phase commit has a famous weakness: a participant that said yes and then lost contact with the coordinator can't decide alone, so it blocks, holding its locks. That's the in-doubt XA transaction a DBA has to resolve by hand. DynamoDB avoids it by making the coordinator's decision durable in the ledger and letting any coordinator finish it. Google Spanner goes further: every participant is itself a Paxos group, so a participant never disappears.

Cassandra's Paxos v2 (4.1 and later) cuts a write to two round trips, by combining the read with the prepare and the commit with the next operation's prepare, roughly. The `cassandra.yaml` of 5.0.9 lists the variants with their round trips: v1 "Expect 4RTs for a write and 3RTs for a read", v2 "Expect 2RTs for a write, and either 1RT or 2RT for a read". To switch, run a full repair on every node, set `paxos_variant: v2` and restart node by node; going back is just as simple.

Notice that Accord's "one round trip in the common case" is a fast path: when replicas agree on the transaction's place in the order straight away, it commits in one round; when concurrent transactions disagree, it falls back to a slower path. That's the same shape as Paxos with a stable leader, and the reason contention costs latency in every one of these systems.

If you want to read one more paper, read Jepsen's MongoDB 4.2.6 report end to end. It shows how a test harness finds lost writes and read skew, and why a database's defaults and its documentation matter as much as its protocol.
